title: Life from Nothing, Tested
paragraphs: For most of recorded history, the idea that living things could arise from nonliving matter was not a superstition but an observation.
Aristotle taught that certain insects and worms sprang from decaying matter, and maggots on meat, frogs in spring mud, and mice in granaries seemed to prove him right.
In the early seventeenth century the Flemish physician Jan Baptist van Helmont, a serious chemist, offered a recipe: wheat sealed in a jar with a sweaty shirt would yield mice in about three weeks.
The doctrine, called spontaneous generation, rested on the oldest evidence there is: seeing something happen and not seeing its cause.
The first real test came in 1668 from Francesco Redi, a physician at the Medici court in Florence.
Redi put pieces of meat, among them snake, fish, eel, and veal, into flasks: some left open, some sealed, and some covered with a fine gauze that let in air but kept out insects.
Maggots appeared in the meat of the open flasks and never in the sealed ones.
The gauze-covered flasks were the telling case: flies, drawn by the smell, laid their eggs on the cloth, and maggots hatched on the gauze but never in the meat below.
Redi concluded that maggots were the young of flies, not the children of rot.
He did not abandon the old doctrine altogether; he allowed that certain worms found inside plants and animals might still arise on their own.
Within a decade the question had changed scale.
In the 1670s Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft cloth merchant who ground superb lenses, reported to the Royal Society that pond water and pepper water swarmed with creatures too small for the eye.
An infusion, in the language of the time, was simply water in which some organic material had been steeped, and such liquids reliably filled with these animalcules within days.
Flies might have parents, but no one had seen these creatures lay eggs, and the doctrine retreated to the microscopic world and made a comfortable home there.
In the 1740s John Needham, an English priest and a Fellow of the Royal Society, tested the matter directly.
He heated mutton gravy, corked it in a flask, and warmed the flask in hot ashes to kill anything the first heating had missed.
After some days the gravy was teeming.

Needham, working alongside the French naturalist Buffon, concluded that heat had destroyed whatever life the broth once held and that a vegetative force in the matter itself had produced the new creatures.
Lazzaro Spallanzani, an Italian priest and one of the most careful experimenters of his century, did not believe it.
In the 1760s he repeated Needham's work with two changes.
He boiled his infusions far longer, for about an hour, and instead of a cork he sealed each flask by melting its glass neck shut.
Nothing grew.
When he cracked a seal and let air reach the broth, the animalcules returned within days.
Needham objected that an hour of boiling had destroyed the vegetative force, and that the air in a sealed, heated flask had been spoiled, so the experiment proved nothing about ordinary air.

His objections are often presented as the excuses of a loser, and I think that is unfair: it is easy to smile at the first, but the second was sound, and it took the better part of a century to answer.
In 1837 Theodor Schwann passed air through a heated tube before letting it reach a boiled broth, and the broth stayed clear.
In the 1850s Heinrich Schroeder and Theodor von Dusch plugged flask necks with cotton wool, which passed air but trapped dust, and most boiled broths stayed clear.
Milk and some meat infusions spoiled anyway, and the doctrine's defenders noticed.
The decisive round opened in 1859, when Felix Pouchet of Rouen published a long treatise defending spontaneous generation with experiments of his own.
The French Academy of Sciences offered a prize for experiments that would settle the question, and Louis Pasteur, fresh from his work on fermentation, entered.
His best known device was the swan-neck flask: boiled broth in a flask whose neck had been drawn out into a long curve that dipped and rose again, open to the air at its far end.
Air could move freely in and out, but the dust it carried settled in the bend and never reached the liquid.
Such broths stayed clear for months; some remain unspoiled today.
Tilt one so the broth washed into the bend, or snap off the neck, and it spoiled within days; the only change was whether dust touched the liquid.
Pasteur also examined the air itself, drawing it through guncotton and finding in the dissolved plug organized bodies that looked like the germs of the microbes spoiling his broths.

Then he carried sealed flasks of boiled broth to places with different air and briefly opened a set in each: in the still air of a cellar beneath the Paris Observatory, on a hill in the Jura, and on the Mer de Glace glacier at about 2,000 meters.
The cleaner the air, the fewer flasks spoiled; on the glacier only one flask in twenty spoiled.
The Academy awarded him its prize in 1862, and in a lecture at the Sorbonne in 1864 he declared that the doctrine would never recover from the blow.
It was a fine piece of theater, and I think it was premature.
Pouchet had worked with hay infusions, while Pasteur worked mostly with sugared yeast water.
Pouchet's boiled hay flasks spoiled repeatedly, and Pasteur, who could not reproduce the result with his own broths, assumed carelessness.
A commission of the Academy set terms for a direct comparison in 1864, but Pouchet withdrew in protest, and the two broths were never tested side by side.
We now know that hay carries bacterial spores that survive boiling at 100 degrees Celsius, so Pouchet's flasks were spoiling for reasons that had nothing to do with carelessness.

In 1870 Thomas Henry Huxley gave the two positions their modern labels, biogenesis for life from life and abiogenesis for life from nonliving matter, and the English physician Henry Charlton Bastian kept defending abiogenesis with boiled infusions of his own.
The man who finished the argument was a physicist.

John Tyndall of the Royal Institution in London had spent years studying how light scatters from dust in the air, and he knew that a beam through a closed box would show the dust as a glowing track until it settled.
In the mid-1870s he built a cabinet with a glass front, coated its inner walls with glycerin to hold whatever landed on them, and waited until a beam showed nothing at all.
Boiled broths in this optically empty air stayed clear for months, while identical broths in ordinary air spoiled within days.
Then the experiment failed.
After he brought old hay into the laboratory, boiled broths began to spoil even in the cabinet, and a single boiling no longer protected them.
Tyndall concluded that some bacteria pass through a resting phase that survives boiling and later wakes, which fit the spores Ferdinand Cohn had described in the hay bacterium in 1876.
His remedy was patient rather than violent: boil briefly, let the broth stand so the resting forms could wake into their vulnerable state, boil again, and repeat several times.
The method, now called discontinuous heating, sterilized broths that an hour of continuous boiling could not.
Looking back over two centuries, what strikes me is how many times the question was answered and how reliably it returned at a smaller scale.

Redi settled it for flies and the microscope reopened it; Spallanzani settled it for sealed flasks and the air objection reopened it; Pasteur settled it for his broths and Pouchet's hay reopened it, whatever he said at the Sorbonne.
Each answer was correct within its limits, and each limit was invisible until someone tested the next case.
The lesson is not that the doctrine's defenders were fools; many were careful, and Needham's complaint about spoiled air was better than the first answers to it.
It is that an experiment proves no more than the hardiest contaminant allows it to prove, and the final word belonged to the person who found that contaminant.

questions.stem: The author mentions van Helmont's recipe for mice in paragraph 1 primarily to
choices: mock the state of chemistry in the early seventeenth century as hopelessly naive
explain why mice were so often discovered in granaries
show that a serious scientist could treat the doctrine as plain observation
introduce the series of flask experiments that Redi performed in 1668
argue that the doctrine was a superstition rather than an observation

proof.quote: a serious chemist, offered a recipe
was not a superstition but an observation

questions.why: Paragraph 1 opens by saying the idea was not a superstition but an observation, then presents van Helmont, a serious chemist, offering a recipe as if it were a fact of nature. The recipe shows how literally and respectably the doctrine was once held.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author calls van Helmont a serious chemist and never mocks the period.
Wrong focus: the granary mice are one of the observations the doctrine rested on, not something the recipe explains.
Wrong paragraph: Redi's experiment is introduced in paragraph 2 as the first real test, not by the recipe.
Reversed: paragraph 1 says the idea was not a superstition but an observation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in Redi's gauze-covered flasks
choices: maggots appeared in the meat because the gauze let in air
flies laid eggs on the cloth and maggots hatched there, not in the meat
no flies came near because the gauze held in the smell of the meat
the meat stayed free of maggots only because the flasks had been sealed shut
maggots appeared in the meat only after the gauze was removed

proof.quote: laid their eggs on the cloth, and maggots hatched on the gauze but never in the meat below

questions.why: Paragraph 2 calls the gauze-covered flasks the telling case: flies, drawn by the smell, laid their eggs on the cloth, and maggots hatched on the gauze but never in the meat below.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the gauze let in air, but paragraph 2 says the maggots never reached the meat.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 says flies were drawn by the smell and laid eggs on the cloth.
Wrong flasks: the sealed flasks were a separate group; the gauze flasks were open to the air.
Outside the passage: Redi never removes the gauze in the account given.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Redi would most likely have agreed with which of the following statements?
choices: Every living creature descends from parents of its own kind.
Maggots can arise from rotting meat whenever flies are kept away from it.
Gauze is a more reliable barrier against insects than a sealed flask is.
The microscope would eventually overturn his conclusion about flies.
Some worms living inside plants or animals may arise without parents.

proof.quote: he allowed that certain worms found inside plants and animals might still arise on their own

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says Redi did not abandon the old doctrine altogether and allowed that certain worms found inside plants and animals might still arise on their own. That is the one statement he is on record as accepting.
distractorNotes: Too strong: Redi kept an exception for worms inside plants and animals, so he did not hold the universal claim.
Reversed: Redi's sealed and gauze-covered flasks showed that keeping flies away prevents maggots.
Outside the passage: Redi used both barriers, and the passage never ranks one above the other.
Outside the passage: the microscope reopened the question in paragraph 3, but nothing says Redi expected it, and his conclusion about flies was never overturned.

questions.stem: As described in paragraph 3, an infusion was
choices: water in which organic material had been steeped
a drop of pond water examined under a hand-ground lens
a broth that had been boiled and sealed inside a glass flask
a liquid corked in a flask and then warmed in hot ashes
Leeuwenhoek's own name for the creatures he saw in water

proof.quote: was simply water in which some organic material had been steeped

questions.why: Paragraph 3 defines the word directly: an infusion, in the language of the time, was simply water in which some organic material had been steeped.
distractorNotes: Half right: pond water was one of the liquids Leeuwenhoek examined, but the definition in paragraph 3 is about steeping organic material.
Wrong paragraph: sealed, boiled broths belong to Spallanzani in paragraph 5.
Wrong paragraph: corking and hot ashes describe Needham's method in paragraph 4.
Wrong word: the creatures were called animalcules; an infusion is the liquid.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Needham concluded from his experiment with mutton gravy that
choices: the cork had failed to keep outside air away from the gravy
the heating had been too brief to kill everything in the broth
the creatures had entered the flask along with the hot ashes
a vegetative force in the matter itself had produced the creatures
flies had laid their eggs in the gravy before the flask had been corked

proof.quote: a vegetative force in the matter itself had produced the new creatures

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says Needham concluded that heat had destroyed whatever life the broth once held and that a vegetative force in the matter itself had produced the new creatures.
distractorNotes: Reversed: Needham believed his cork and his heating had excluded outside life; the complaint about air came later and in a different form.
Reversed: Needham believed the heat had destroyed whatever life the broth held.
Outside the passage: the ashes were used to heat the corked flask, and no one blamed them.
Wrong paragraph: flies and eggs belong to Redi in paragraph 2; Needham's creatures were microscopic.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of Spallanzani's experiments EXCEPT:
choices: He boiled his infusions for about an hour.
He passed heated air into each flask before sealing it.
He sealed each flask by melting its glass neck shut.
He found that nothing grew in the boiled, sealed flasks.
He saw animalcules return after cracking a seal.

proof.quote: He boiled his infusions far longer, for about an hour
he sealed each flask by melting its glass neck shut
Nothing grew.
the animalcules returned within days
In 1837 Theodor Schwann passed air through a heated tube

questions.why: Paragraph 5 gives Spallanzani's two changes, longer boiling and a melted seal, and his two results, nothing grew and the animalcules returned when a seal was cracked. Heated air belongs to Schwann in paragraph 6, seventy years later.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 says he boiled his infusions far longer, for about an hour.
Paragraph 5 says he sealed each flask by melting its glass neck shut.
Paragraph 5 says plainly that nothing grew.
Paragraph 5 says that when he cracked a seal the animalcules returned within days.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 6, the word 'sound' most nearly means
choices: loud enough to be heard clearly
deep and unbroken, as sleep can be
undamaged by the heat of boiling
stated at length and with feeling
well reasoned and hard to dismiss

proof.quote: the second was sound, and it took the better part of a century to answer

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the second objection was sound and took the better part of a century to answer: an objection that is valid and hard to dismiss. The everyday meanings of the word, noise or deep sleep, do not fit a sentence about an argument.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday noise meaning of the word, and nothing in the sentence is about hearing.
A sound sleep is another common sense, but the sentence is about an objection, not rest.
Too literal: the sentence is about the quality of an argument, not about what heat did to anything.
Nothing in paragraph 6 says how forcefully or at what length Needham made the objection.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Needham's objections in paragraph 6 is best described as
choices: dismissive
amused
respectful
alarmed
indifferent

proof.quote: I think that is unfair
Needham's complaint about spoiled air was better than the first answers to it

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the objections are often presented as the excuses of a loser and that the author finds that unfair, then credits the second objection as sound. Paragraph 11 adds that Needham's complaint was better than the first answers to it. That is respect for an opponent, not scorn.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author objects to dismissing Needham and calls one objection sound.
Wrong register: the author admits it is easy to smile at the first objection and then declines to.
Wrong register: the author's judgment is calm, and no danger is involved.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position in Needham's defense.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a swan-neck flask kept its broth clear because
choices: dust in the air that entered settled in the bend of the neck
the curved neck was melted shut once the broth had been boiled
the broth was boiled far longer than in any earlier experiment
a plug of cotton wool in the neck trapped the dust in the air
air was unable to pass through the long curve of the neck

proof.quote: the dust it carried settled in the bend and never reached the liquid

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says air could move freely in and out of the swan-neck flask, but the dust it carried settled in the bend and never reached the liquid.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: melting the neck shut was Spallanzani's method in paragraph 5; the swan neck stayed open at its far end.
Outside the passage: paragraph 7 says nothing about how long Pasteur boiled, and boiling time was Spallanzani's variable.
Wrong paragraph: cotton wool plugs belong to Schroeder and von Dusch in paragraph 6.
Reversed: paragraph 7 says air could move freely in and out.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when Pasteur opened flasks of boiled broth on the Mer de Glace,
choices: every flask spoiled within days
about half of the flasks spoiled
none of the flasks spoiled at all
only one flask in twenty spoiled
all but one of the flasks spoiled

proof.quote: on the glacier only one flask in twenty spoiled

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the cleaner the air, the fewer flasks spoiled, and that on the glacier only one flask in twenty spoiled.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the glacier had the cleanest air and the fewest spoiled flasks.
Wrong number: paragraph 8 gives one in twenty, not half.
Too strong: one flask did spoil.
Reversed: one spoiled and the rest stayed clear.

questions.stem: The author contrasts Pouchet's hay infusions with Pasteur's yeast water in paragraph 9 primarily to
choices: show that Pasteur's broths spoiled more easily than Pouchet's
explain how both men could have reported their results honestly
argue that the Academy should have awarded its prize to Pouchet
demonstrate that hay is a poor material for preparing an infusion
suggest that Pasteur chose a broth he knew in advance would not spoil

proof.quote: Pouchet's flasks were spoiling for reasons that had nothing to do with carelessness
assumed carelessness

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says Pasteur assumed carelessness, then explains that hay carries spores that survive boiling, so Pouchet's flasks were spoiling for reasons that had nothing to do with carelessness. The contrast in broths accounts for the contradictory results without calling either man dishonest.
distractorNotes: Reversed: it was Pouchet's hay flasks that spoiled repeatedly.
Outside the passage: the author calls Pasteur's declaration premature but never says the prize was wrongly awarded.
Wrong focus: hay's spores explain Pouchet's results; the author is not giving advice on making infusions.
Too strong: paragraph 9 says Pasteur could not reproduce the result and assumed carelessness, not that he chose his broth to win.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if Pouchet had boiled sugared yeast water instead of hay infusions, his flasks would most likely have
choices: stayed clear, as Pasteur's own flasks did
spoiled even sooner than his hay flasks did
spoiled only when opened at low altitude
been accepted by the commission in 1864
shown spores under the microscope

proof.quote: hay carries bacterial spores that survive boiling
Pasteur, who could not reproduce the result with his own broths

questions.why: Paragraph 9 traces Pouchet's spoiled flasks to spores in hay that survive boiling, and says Pasteur could not reproduce the spoiling with his own broths. Take away the hay and the spores go with it.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the hay was the source of the spoiling.
Mixed up: altitude belongs to Pasteur's field trip in paragraph 8, not to Pouchet's broths.
Outside the passage: Pouchet withdrew before any comparison, and the commission never judged his flasks.
Outside the passage: nothing says Pouchet examined spores, and yeast water is the broth without them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Thomas Henry Huxley
choices: defended abiogenesis with boiled infusions of his own
served on the Academy commission that Pouchet refused
first described the spores of the hay bacterium
gave the two sides of the debate their modern names
awarded Pasteur the Academy's prize in 1862

proof.quote: In 1870 Thomas Henry Huxley gave the two positions their modern labels

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says that in 1870 Huxley gave the two positions their modern labels, biogenesis and abiogenesis.
distractorNotes: Wrong person: paragraph 9 gives that role to Henry Charlton Bastian.
Wrong country and paragraph: the commission was French and met in 1864; Huxley is not connected to it.
Wrong person: paragraph 10 credits Ferdinand Cohn with describing the spores.
Wrong body: the French Academy of Sciences awarded the prize.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage in connection with Tyndall's cabinet?
choices: a glass front
inner walls coated with glycerin
a beam of light used to test the air inside
boiled broths that stayed clear for months
flask necks plugged with cotton wool

proof.quote: a cabinet with a glass front
coated its inner walls with glycerin
waited until a beam showed nothing at all
stayed clear for months
plugged flask necks with cotton wool

questions.why: Paragraph 10 describes the cabinet: a glass front, glycerin on the inner walls, a beam of light to test the air, and broths that stayed clear for months inside it. Cotton wool plugs belong to Schroeder and von Dusch in paragraph 6.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10 says he built a cabinet with a glass front.
Paragraph 10 says he coated its inner walls with glycerin.
Paragraph 10 says he waited until a beam of light showed nothing at all.
Paragraph 10 says broths in the optically empty air stayed clear for months.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Tyndall's broths began to spoil inside the cabinet after the hay arrived because
choices: the glycerin on the walls had lost its grip on the settling dust
the beam of light could no longer be seen clearly through the glass front
the air now carried resting forms that one boiling could not kill
the hay had been steeped in water for too short a time
the glass front of the cabinet had been left open to the room

proof.quote: a single boiling no longer protected them
some bacteria pass through a resting phase that survives boiling and later wakes

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says that after the hay arrived, boiled broths spoiled even in the cabinet and a single boiling no longer protected them, and Tyndall concluded that some bacteria pass through a resting phase that survives boiling. The hay had brought those forms into the room.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing says the glycerin stopped working.
Outside the passage: the beam test is never said to fail.
Outside the passage: no steeping time is given, and the problem was in the broths, not the hay.
Outside the passage: no door or opening is mentioned, and the broths spoiled even in the cabinet.

questions.stem: A cannery seals jars of vegetables after one continuous hour of boiling, yet some jars still spoil. Which change does the reasoning in paragraph 10 most strongly support?
choices: Boil the jars for three continuous hours instead of one before sealing them.
Boil the jars briefly, let them stand, and boil again, repeating the cycle.
Filter the air of the cannery through cotton wool before sealing the jars.
Coat the inner walls of the cannery with glycerin so dust settles out of the air.
Move the cannery to a high mountain where the air carries fewer germs.

proof.quote: boil briefly, let the broth stand so the resting forms could wake into their vulnerable state, boil again, and repeat several times
sterilized broths that an hour of continuous boiling could not

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says Tyndall's remedy was to boil briefly, let the broth stand so the resting forms could wake into their vulnerable state, boil again, and repeat, and that this sterilized broths that an hour of continuous boiling could not. Jars that survive an hour of boiling and still spoil are the same problem.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 10 says the resting forms survive an hour of continuous boiling, so more of the same is not the remedy.
Wrong mechanism: cotton wool in paragraph 6 keeps dust out of the air, but the problem here is a form already inside the jar that survives boiling.
Wrong mechanism: the glycerin in paragraph 10 settles dust from the air; it does not kill what is already in the broth.
Wrong mechanism: cleaner air in paragraph 8 means fewer flasks get contaminated, but these jars are sealed and already hold forms that survive boiling.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks were the single decisive experiment that ended belief in spontaneous generation once and for all.
The defenders of spontaneous generation were careless experimenters whose results could never be reproduced by others.
The microscope made the question of spontaneous generation impossible to answer by experiment alone.
The question was answered repeatedly at one scale and returned at a smaller one until heat-resistant spores were found.
Tyndall's discontinuous heating mattered more to the practice of medicine than any of Pasteur's experiments with flasks.

proof.quote: how many times the question was answered and how reliably it returned at a smaller scale
an experiment proves no more than the hardiest contaminant allows it to prove
I think it was premature

questions.why: Paragraph 11 states it outright: the question was answered many times and reliably returned at a smaller scale, and the final word belonged to the person who found the hardiest contaminant. The whole passage, from Redi to Tyndall, is built to make that case.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 9 calls Pasteur's declaration premature, and paragraph 11 says Pouchet's hay reopened the question.
Contradicted: paragraph 11 says many defenders were careful, and paragraph 9 clears Pouchet of carelessness.
Too strong: the microscope reopened the question in paragraph 3, but experiments went on answering it.
Outside the passage: the author admires Tyndall's result but never ranks it against Pasteur for medicine.
